evidence: Supported by citations to established literature (Eisenbarth, 2019; Mass et al., 2016; Doebel et al., 2017).

claim: Around 80% of CD1a+CD207+ rLCs express RTN1A.
source: Around 80% of CD1a+CD207+ rLCs and eLCs express RTN1A (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Around 80% of CD1a+CD207+ eLCs express RTN1A.
source: Around 80% of CD1a+CD207+ rLCs and eLCs express RTN1A (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The untagged α-RTN1A ab was detected in the cell body and in the dendrites of rLCs after 3 hr of cultivation.
source: The untagged α-RTN1A ab was detected with a fluorescently labeled secondary ab in the cell body and in the dendrites of rLCs already after only 3 hr, more pronounced at 6 hr and most prominent in the majority of rLCs at 24 hr of cultivation, while the isotype signal was substantially weaker (6 hr) or undetectable (3 and 24 hr) (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1B and C.

claim: A prominent roundish morphology of rLCs was observed after 24 hr of incubation with the α-RTN1A abs in comparison to isotype-treated epidermis.
source: A prominent roundish morphology of rLCs was observed after 24 hr of incubation with the α-RTN1A abs in comparison to isotype-treated epidermis.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1C and quantified in Figure 1E-F.

claim: Not all rLCs captured the α-RTN1A ab during the culture period.
source: Notably, not all rLCs did so (Figure 1C, white arrows).
evidence: Observation from immunofluorescence images in Figure 1C.

claim: Not all rLCs and eLCs express RTN1A.
source: Indeed, not all rLCs and eLCs express RTN1A to which the ab could have bound during the culture period.
evidence: Inference from the observation that not all cells captured the antibody and flow cytometry data showing ~80% expression.

claim: ~70% of RTN1A+ rLCs co-express CD207.
source: Gating of RTN1A+ cells according to LC marker expression revealed that ~70% and ~80% of rLCs co-express CD207 and CD1a, respectively (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: ~80% of RTN1A+ rLCs co-express CD1a.
source: Gating of RTN1A+ cells according to LC marker expression revealed that ~70% and ~80% of rLCs co-express CD207 and CD1a, respectively (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: ~70% of RTN1A+ eLCs co-express CD207.
source: A similar observation was found for eLCs (~70% of RTN1A+ eLCs co-express CD207 or CD1a; Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: ~70% of RTN1A+ eLCs co-express CD1a.
source: A similar observation was found for eLCs (~70% of RTN1A+ eLCs co-express CD207 or CD1a; Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: RTN1A co-localizes with vimentin in the cell body and in the most distant tips of dendrites in untreated epidermal sheets.
source: Images of untreated (UT) epidermal sheets cultured for 24 hr showed co-localization of RTN1A with vimentin in the cell body and in the most distant tips of dendrites with dot-like RTN1A accumulations (Figure 1D, pinkish arrows), whereas CD207 expression was detected at lower intensity and mainly the cell body (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Inhibition of RTN1A caused a significant decrease in the number of dendritic rLCs after 24 hr of incubation compared to controls.
source: Enumeration of dendritic and roundish rLCs within epidermal biopsy punches after 24 hr of incubation with or without abs showed a significant decrease in the number (Figure 1E) and percentage (UT: 71.47; isotype: 63.52; α-RTN1A ab: 39.74; Figure 1F) of dendritic rLCs after blocking of RTN1A in comparison to controls.
evidence: Supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1E and F.

claim: Inhibition of RTN1A caused a significant increase of roundish rLCs after 24 hr of incubation compared to controls.
source: This observation correlates with a significant increase of roundish rLCs (UT: 28.53; isotype: 36.48; α-RTN1A ab: 60.26; Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Inhibition of RTN1A caused significant dendrite retraction in rLCs compared with those in isotype and UT epidermal sheets.
source: Quantification of the dendrite lengths in 3D fluorescent images of cultures epidermal sheets revealed that inhibition of RTN1A caused significant dendrite retraction in rLCs compared with those in isotype and UT epidermal sheets (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of dendrite lengths shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Sholl analysis showed significantly decreased rLC dendrite distribution in isotype- and α-RTN1A ab-treated epidermal sheets in comparison to UT epidermal sheets.
source: Application of this analysis for rLCs in epidermal sheets showed significantly decreased rLC dendrite distribution in isotype- and α-RTN1A ab-treated epidermal sheets in comparison to UT epidermal sheets (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by Sholl analysis data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The difference in dendrite distribution between isotype- and α-RTN1A ab-treated epidermal sheets was not significant.
source: Of note, the difference between isotype- and α-RTN1A ab-treated epidermal sheets was not significant, indicating that the inhibition of RTN1A affected the length of rLC dendrites but not the frequency and complexity (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by Sholl analysis data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Inhibition of RTN1A affected the length of rLC dendrites but not the frequency and complexity.
source: Of note, the difference between isotype- and α-RTN1A ab-treated epidermal sheets was not significant, indicating that the inhibition of RTN1A affected the length of rLC dendrites but not the frequency and complexity (Figure 2C).
evidence: Inference drawn from Sholl analysis data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: There was a significant decrease in the migration potential of LCs in culture wells containing α-RTN1A ab-treated compared to isotype-treated epidermal sheets after 24 hr of cultivation.
source: We found a significant decrease in the migration potential of LCs in culture wells containing α-RTN1A ab-treated compared to isotype-treated epidermal sheets after 24 hr of cultivation (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by enumeration of eLCs shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Ab uptake was detected in eLCs at all investigated time points.
source: Similar to rLCs (Figure 1B and C), ab uptake was also detected in eLCs at all investigated time points, with a tendency of a more pronounced though not significantly higher signal of RTN1A ab compared to the isotype (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The CD1a expression level (MFI) was significantly reduced in eLCs after α-RTN1A ab treatment.
source: We found that the CD1a expression level (mean fluorescence intensity [MFI]), but not the percentage of CD1a+ eLCs, was significantly reduced after α-RTN1A ab treatment, whereas CD207 expression was unchanged.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The percentage of CD1a+ eLCs was not significantly changed after α-RTN1A ab treatment.
source: We found that the CD1a expression level (mean fluorescence intensity [MFI]), but not the percentage of CD1a+ eLCs, was significantly reduced after α-RTN1A ab treatment, whereas CD207 expression was unchanged.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: CD207 expression in eLCs was unchanged after α-RTN1A ab treatment.
source: We found that the CD1a expression level (mean fluorescence intensity [MFI]), but not the percentage of CD1a+ eLCs, was significantly reduced after α-RTN1A ab treatment, whereas CD207 expression was unchanged.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Inhibition of RTN1A caused a significant increase in the percentage and expression intensity of CCR7 in eLCs.
source: Here, the inhibition of RTN1A caused a significant increase in the percentage and expression intensity of CCR7, and a decrease of CD86 in comparison to controls.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Inhibition of RTN1A caused a decrease of CD86 in eLCs in comparison to controls.
source: Here, the inhibition of RTN1A caused a significant increase in the percentage and expression intensity of CCR7, and a decrease of CD86 in comparison to controls.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Inhibition of RTN1A endorses acquisition of the migratory phenotype by LCs.
source: These results suggest that inhibition of RTN1A endorse acquisition of the migratory phenotype by LCs, along with preventing the maturation of some LCs.
evidence: Inference drawn from CCR7 and CD86 expression data in Figure 3C.

claim: Inhibition of RTN1A prevents the maturation of some LCs.
source: These results suggest that inhibition of RTN1A endorse acquisition of the migratory phenotype by LCs, along with preventing the maturation of some LCs.
evidence: Inference drawn from CCR7 and CD86 expression data in Figure 3C.

claim: Treatment of epidermal sheets with the α-RTN1A ab for 24 hr significantly decreased the concentrations of CD44 in culture supernatants in comparison with controls.
source: Treatment of epidermal sheets with the α-RTN1A ab for 24 hr significantly decreased the concentrations of CD44, PECAM-1, NCAM, ALCAM, and EpCAM but not L-selectin in culture supernatants in comparison with controls (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by LEGENDplex bead array data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Treatment of epidermal sheets with the α-RTN1A ab for 24 hr significantly decreased the concentrations of PECAM-1 in culture supernatants in comparison with controls.
source: Treatment of epidermal sheets with the α-RTN1A ab for 24 hr significantly decreased the concentrations of CD44, PECAM-1, NCAM, ALCAM, and EpCAM but not L-selectin in culture supernatants in comparison with controls (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by LEGENDplex bead array data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Treatment of epidermal sheets with the α-RTN1A ab for 24 hr significantly decreased the concentrations of NCAM in culture supernatants in comparison with controls.

claim: Treatment of epidermal sheets with the α-RTN1A ab for 24 hr significantly decreased the concentrations of EpCAM in culture supernatants in comparison with controls.
source: Treatment of epidermal sheets with the α-RTN1A ab for 24 hr significantly decreased the concentrations of CD44, PECAM-1, NCAM, ALCAM, and EpCAM but not L-selectin in culture supernatants in comparison with controls (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by LEGENDplex bead array data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Treatment of epidermal sheets with the α-RTN1A ab for 24 hr did not significantly change the concentration of L-selectin in culture supernatants in comparison with controls.
source: Treatment of epidermal sheets with the α-RTN1A ab for 24 hr significantly decreased the concentrations of CD44, PECAM-1, NCAM, ALCAM, and EpCAM but not L-selectin in culture supernatants in comparison with controls (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by LEGENDplex bead array data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The detachment of rLCs from the tissue was hampered by α-RTN1A ab treatment.
source: These data suggest that the detachment of rLCs from the tissue was hampered.
evidence: Inference drawn from adhesion molecule data in Figure 3D and migration data in Figure 3A.

claim: THP-1 RTN1A+ cells were significantly smaller in size compared to THP-1 wt cells.
source: THP-1 RTN1A+ cell morphology was considerably altered compared to THP-1 wt cells as they were significantly smaller in size and had markedly more condensed intermediate filament structures as visualized by vimentin staining (Figure 4B, C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by cell area measurements shown in Figure 4C.

claim: THP-1 RTN1A+ cells had markedly more condensed intermediate filament structures compared to THP-1 wt cells.
source: THP-1 RTN1A+ cell morphology was considerably altered compared to THP-1 wt cells as they were significantly smaller in size and had markedly more condensed intermediate filament structures as visualized by vimentin staining (Figure 4B, C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence images shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: RTN1A significantly co-localized with vimentin at the bottom and top of THP-1 RTN1A+ cells.
source: We found a significant overlap between RTN1A and vimentin at the bottom and top of the cell (Figure 4D, E), whereas there was less co-localization with F-actin in the same cell compartments (Figure 4D, E).
evidence: Supported by co-localization analysis using Manders' coefficient shown in Figure 4D and E.

claim: There was less co-localization between RTN1A and F-actin at the bottom and top of THP-1 RTN1A+ cells.
source: We found a significant overlap between RTN1A and vimentin at the bottom and top of the cell (Figure 4D, E), whereas there was less co-localization with F-actin in the same cell compartments (Figure 4D, E).
evidence: Supported by co-localization analysis using Manders' coefficient shown in Figure 4D and E.

claim: In the middle part of THP-1 RTN1A+ cells, RTN1A showed similar co-localization levels with F-actin and vimentin.
source: In the middle part of the cell, RTN1A showed similar co-localization levels with F-actin and vimentin (Figure 4D, E).
evidence: Supported by co-localization analysis using Manders' coefficient shown in Figure 4D and E.

claim: THP-1 RTN1A+ cells displayed a significantly lower proliferation rate compared with THP-1 wt control.
source: Indeed, THP-1 RTN1A+ cells displayed a significantly lower proliferation rate, CFSE dye dilution, and cell number compared with THP-1 wt control (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by proliferation assay data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: THP-1 RTN1A+ cells displayed significantly lower CFSE dye dilution compared with THP-1 wt control.
source: Indeed, THP-1 RTN1A+ cells displayed a significantly lower proliferation rate, CFSE dye dilution, and cell number compared with THP-1 wt control (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by CFSE dilution data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: THP-1 RTN1A+ cells displayed significantly lower cell number compared with THP-1 wt control.
source: Indeed, THP-1 RTN1A+ cells displayed a significantly lower proliferation rate, CFSE dye dilution, and cell number compared with THP-1 wt control (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by cell counting data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Expression of RTN1A in THP-1 Mφs resulted in significantly larger cell bodies compared with THP-1 wt Mφs.
source: Expression of RTN1A in THP-1 Mφs resulted in altered morphology with significantly larger cell bodies and substantially longer cell protrusions when compared with THP-1 wt Mφs (Figure 5B–D).
evidence: Supported by cell body size measurements shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Expression of RTN1A in THP-1 Mφs resulted in substantially longer cell protrusions compared with THP-1 wt Mφs.
source: Expression of RTN1A in THP-1 Mφs resulted in altered morphology with significantly larger cell bodies and substantially longer cell protrusions when compared with THP-1 wt Mφs (Figure 5B–D).
evidence: Supported by cell protrusion length measurements shown in Figure 5D.

claim: In THP-1 Mφs, RTN1A significantly co-localized with vimentin.
source: Alike in undifferentiated THP-1 cells (Figure 4D, E), RTN1A significantly co-localized with vimentin and to a lesser extent with F-actin (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by co-localization analysis shown in Figure 5E.

claim: In THP-1 Mφs, RTN1A co-localized to a lesser extent with F-actin.
source: Alike in undifferentiated THP-1 cells (Figure 4D, E), RTN1A significantly co-localized with vimentin and to a lesser extent with F-actin (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by co-localization analysis shown in Figure 5E.

claim: THP-1 RTN1A+ cells display an increased capacity in cellular aggregate formation compared with THP-1 wt cells.
source: We discovered that THP-1 RTN1A+ cells display an increased capacity in cellular aggregate formation compared with THP-1 wt cells (Figure 5F and G and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by aggregate enumeration data shown in Figure 5F and G.

claim: Supernatants of THP-1 RTN1A+ cells showed increased NCAM compared to THP-1 wt cells.
source: We found increased NCAM and PECAM-1 and significantly decreased ALCAM concentrations in supernatants of THP-1 RTN1A+ in comparison to THP-1 wt cells (Figure 5H).
evidence: Supported by LEGENDplex bead array data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: Supernatants of THP-1 RTN1A+ cells showed increased PECAM-1 compared to THP-1 wt cells.
source: We found increased NCAM and PECAM-1 and significantly decreased ALCAM concentrations in supernatants of THP-1 RTN1A+ in comparison to THP-1 wt cells (Figure 5H).
evidence: Supported by LEGENDplex bead array data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: Supernatants of THP-1 RTN1A+ cells showed significantly decreased ALCAM concentrations compared to THP-1 wt cells.
source: We found increased NCAM and PECAM-1 and significantly decreased ALCAM concentrations in supernatants of THP-1 RTN1A+ in comparison to THP-1 wt cells (Figure 5H).
evidence: Supported by LEGENDplex bead array data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: Both the early and late response to ionomycin in THP-1 RTN1A+ cells was significantly lower in comparison to the calcium flux in THP-1 wt cells.
source: Both the early and late response to ionomycin in THP-1 RTN1A+ cells was significantly lower in comparison to the calcium flux in THP-1 wt cells (Figure 5I).
evidence: Supported by ratiometric calcium flux measurements shown in Figure 5I.

claim: Cell stimulation with thapsigargin caused significantly lower Ca2+ efflux from the ER store in the early and late phase of the measurement in THP-1 RTN1A+ cells.
source: Cell stimulation with thapsigargin caused significantly lower Ca2+ efflux from the ER store in the early and late phase of the measurement in THP-1 RTN1A+ cells (Figure 5J).
evidence: Supported by ratiometric calcium flux measurements shown in Figure 5J.

claim: RTN1A has an inhibitory effect on the Ca2+ efflux from ER in comparison to THP-1 wt cells.
source: The results show that RTN1A has an inhibitory effect on the Ca2+ efflux from ER in comparison to THP-1 wt cells and most likely results in a decreased Ca2+ influx through the plasma membrane.
evidence: Inference drawn from calcium flux measurements shown in Figure 5I and J.

claim: RTN1A most likely results in a decreased Ca2+ influx through the plasma membrane.
source: The results show that RTN1A has an inhibitory effect on the Ca2+ efflux from ER in comparison to THP-1 wt cells and most likely results in a decreased Ca2+ influx through the plasma membrane.
evidence: Inference drawn from calcium flux measurements shown in Figure 5I and J.

claim: RTN1A expression may induce a feedback regulatory mechanism to counteract elevated cell adhesion.
source: Together, our data suggest that RTN1A expression may induce a feedback regulatory mechanism to counteract elevated cell adhesion and further highlights a potential role of RTN1A in fine-tuning cell activation and adhesion.
evidence: Inference drawn from adhesion molecule and calcium flux data in Figure 5.

claim: RTN1A has a potential role in fine-tuning cell activation and adhesion.
source: Together, our data suggest that RTN1A expression may induce a feedback regulatory mechanism to counteract elevated cell adhesion and further highlights a potential role of RTN1A in fine-tuning cell activation and adhesion.
evidence: Inference drawn from adhesion molecule and calcium flux data in Figure 5.

claim: Both the percentage of RTN1A+ eLCs and RTN1A expression intensity in eLCs were significantly diminished after activation with TLR1/2 agonist (Pam3CSK4).
source: Incubation of epidermal explants with selected extra- and intracellular TLR agonists and subsequent analysis of eLCs by flow cytometry (Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A) revealed that both the percentage of RTN1A+ eLCs and RTN1A expression intensity in eLCs were significantly diminished after activation with the agonists TLR1/2 (Pam3CSK4), TLR2 (Listeria monocytogenes), and TLR7 (imiquimod, polyadenylic:polyuridylic acid (poly(A:U)), but not to agonists of TLR2/6 [mycoplasma salivarium] and TLR3 [low and high molecular weight polyinosinic:polycytidylic acid, LMW and HMW poly(I:C)]) (Figure 6B–D).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6B-D.

claim: Both the percentage of RTN1A+ eLCs and RTN1A expression intensity in eLCs were significantly diminished after activation with TLR2 agonist (Listeria monocytogenes).
source: Incubation of epidermal explants with selected extra- and intracellular TLR agonists and subsequent analysis of eLCs by flow cytometry (Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A) revealed that both the percentage of RTN1A+ eLCs and RTN1A expression intensity in eLCs were significantly diminished after activation with the agonists TLR1/2 (Pam3CSK4), TLR2 (Listeria monocytogenes), and TLR7 (imiquimod, polyadenylic:polyuridylic acid (poly(A:U)), but not to agonists of TLR2/6 [mycoplasma salivarium] and TLR3 [low and high molecular weight polyinosinic:polycytidylic acid, LMW and HMW poly(I:C)]) (Figure 6B–D).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6B-D.

claim: Both the percentage of RTN1A+ eLCs and RTN1A expression intensity in eLCs were significantly diminished after activation with TLR7 agonists (imiquimod, poly(A:U)).

claim: Human LCs express TLR1/2 for detection of bacterial lipids.
source: Human LCs express a particular repertoire of extracellular TLRs such as TLR1/2, TLR2 (Flacher et al., 2006) for detection of bacterial lipids, and intracellular TLR7 (van der Aar et al., 2007) but not TLR3 (Tajpara et al., 2018) for recognition of viral RNA.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Flacher et al., 2006).

evidence: Speculation based on TLR activation mechanisms and RTN1A downregulation data, supported by citations (Kim et al., 2016; Latz et al., 2004).
